hook: Graphs on the exam are rarely smooth curves. They come with holes, jumps, filled and open dots, and asymptotes, and most limit questions are about exactly those places. Reading a graph's limits is a skill of looking at each side separately. Once you can do that, every limit question on a graph takes seconds.

prereq.why: Input heads to 2, outputs head to 6; the value $f(2)$ is not involved.

prereq.q: A graph has a filled dot at $(3, 1)$ and an open circle at $(3, 4)$. What is $f(3)$?
prereq.why: The filled dot is on the graph.

figure.caption: Four behaviors as $x$ approaches 1: a hole (limit 2), a jump (no limit), unbounded outputs (no limit), oscillation (no limit).

chain.cause: Slide $x$ toward $a$ from the left only
chain.effect: the heights give the left-hand limit, $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)$

chain.cause: Slide $x$ toward $a$ from the right only
chain.effect: the heights give the right-hand limit, $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$

chain.cause: Both one-sided limits exist and are equal
chain.effect: the two-sided limit exists and equals that number

chain.cause: The sides disagree, the outputs are unbounded, or they oscillate

ideas: $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)$ uses only $x < a$; $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$ uses only $x > a$. Follow the graph's heights on that side to the edge at $x = a$.
$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ exactly when both one-sided limits equal $L$.
A limit fails to exist when the one-sided limits differ (a jump), when the outputs grow without bound, or when they oscillate.
Filled and open dots tell you $f(a)$; they never decide the limit.
A justification names both one-sided limits: "From the left $f(x) \to 3$; from the right $f(x) \to 1$; since $3 \ne 1$, the limit does not exist."

misconception.wrong: If $f(a)$ is not defined, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ does not exist.
misconception.right: A missing value never decides a limit. A hole has a limit (the height it sits at) and no value. Decide existence only from the two one-sided limits.

summary: Read a graph's limit one side at a time. The left-hand and right-hand limits are the heights the graph heads to from each side. If they exist and agree, that is the limit; if they differ, or the outputs are unbounded or oscillate, the limit does not exist. Dots give the value $f(a)$, which never affects the limit.
